# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological advances, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and subsequently drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the clinical success of contemporary DES, concerns persist regarding the permanent presence of a metallic prosthesis, including chronic inflammation, impaired vasomotion, late stent thrombosis, and the limitation of future revascularization options [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide transient mechanical support during vessel healing, followed by complete resorption, theoretically restoring native vascular function [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, clinical evidence, and ultimate decline of BVS technology.

## Concept and Device Design

The central premise of BVS is "vascular restoration therapy," whereby the scaffold maintains vessel patency during the critical early healing period and then dissolves, eliminating the long-term risks of a permanent implant [5]. The most extensively studied device was the Absorb everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactide (PLLA) scaffold (Abbott Vascular) [6]. Other platforms included magnesium-based scaffolds (Magmaris) and various polymer-based designs [7]. The PLLA backbone degrades via hydrolysis to lactic acid, which is metabolized through the Krebs cycle, with full resorption typically occurring over approximately three years [8]. Potential benefits hypothesized included restoration of vasomotor function, late luminal enlargement, and freedom from the need for prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy [9].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human ABSORB cohort A study demonstrated feasibility and acceptable short-term outcomes with the first-generation device [10]. The subsequent cohort B confirmed scaffold resorption and restoration of vasomotion on serial imaging [11]. These promising early results prompted larger randomized trials comparing BVS to metallic DES, particularly the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting Xience stent [12]. Imaging studies using optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound provided detailed insights into scaffold healing and strut coverage [13].

## Randomized Trials and Meta-Analyses

The ABSORB II trial randomized patients to the Absorb BVS versus the Xience stent, but failed to demonstrate superiority in vasomotor reactivity and showed inferior late lumen outcomes [14]. The ABSORB III trial, a large pivotal study, established non-inferiority for target lesion failure at one year, supporting initial regulatory approval [15]. However, the ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China trials also showed comparable early outcomes while signaling concerns about scaffold thrombosis [16,17]. The AIDA trial similarly raised safety concerns in a real-world population [18].

As longer-term data accrued, multiple meta-analyses revealed an increased risk of device thrombosis with BVS compared with metallic DES, particularly very late scaffold thrombosis occurring beyond one year [19,20]. The excess risk became more apparent with extended follow-up, undermining the central rationale of the technology [21]. Pooled analyses of the ABSORB trials confirmed a higher rate of target lesion failure and device thrombosis at three years [22].

## Mechanisms of Failure

Several mechanisms were proposed to explain BVS failure. The relatively thick struts (approximately 150 μm) compared with contemporary DES contributed to disturbed flow, delayed endothelialization, and thrombogenicity [23]. Suboptimal implantation technique, including inadequate lesion preparation, undersizing, and insufficient post-dilatation, was strongly associated with adverse outcomes [24]. Scaffold discontinuity and late strut malapposition during the resorption process were implicated in very late thrombotic events identified on intracoronary imaging [25]. The recognition of these issues prompted the development of optimized implantation protocols emphasizing the "PSP" technique—adequate preparation, appropriate sizing, and post-dilatation [26].

## Clinical Decline and Lessons Learned

In light of the cumulative safety signals, the Absorb device was withdrawn from commercial markets in 2017 [27]. Extended follow-up from pivotal trials continued to inform the field, with some analyses suggesting that the excess risk attenuated after complete resorption, raising the possibility that improved devices and technique might yet succeed [28]. Next-generation thinner-strut bioresorbable scaffolds and magnesium-based platforms remain under investigation, with the hope of preserving the conceptual benefits while mitigating thrombotic risk [29]. The BVS experience underscores the importance of rigorous long-term evaluation, careful patient and lesion selection, and meticulous implantation technique in the adoption of novel coronary technologies [30].

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represented an innovative concept aimed at transient vessel support and eventual restoration of native coronary physiology. Despite encouraging early results, randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrated increased rates of scaffold thrombosis and target lesion failure, leading to withdrawal of the first-generation device. The lessons learned continue to guide the development of improved bioresorbable technologies, which may ultimately fulfill the original promise if thrombotic risks can be overcome through superior design and optimized implantation.
